period: Rising from Dynasty 2; state god from Dynasty 5, c. 2494 BC
summary: Every night the sun died in the west, sailed through the underworld fighting a giant snake, and was reborn at dawn. Royal tombs are maps of that voyage.
look: Ra is the falcon-headed man with a sun disc ringed by a cobra on his head. At dawn he is Khepri, a scarab beetle pushing the sun; at dusk he is Atum, an old man; at night he is a ram-headed figure standing in a boat. You will meet his night voyage on the walls of the Valley of the Kings on the 21st, and Ra-Horakhty in Abu Simbel's sanctuary and above its entrance on the 17th.
story:
His home was Iunu, which the Greeks called Heliopolis, 'sun city', now buried under north-east Cairo. From the 4th Dynasty every king was 'Son of Ra', and 5th Dynasty kings built him sun temples at Abusir. Other gods were drawn into his orbit: Amun-Ra at Thebes, and Ra-Horakhty, 'Ra who is Horus of the Two Horizons', the rising sun.

The sun lived a life every day. At dawn he was Khepri, the scarab, 'he who comes into being'. At noon he was Ra in full strength, crossing the sky in his day barque. At sunset, old as Atum, he passed through the western horizon into the Duat, the underworld, aboard his night barque. Through twelve hours and twelve regions he sailed a hidden river, woke the dead, merged with Osiris and fought Apophis, the chaos serpent, who tried to swallow the boat or freeze it with his stare. Seth stood in the prow and speared him. At dawn the sun was reborn, often from the body of the sky goddess Nut. New Kingdom royal tombs carry this journey on their walls, in texts such as the Amduat, 'what is in the underworld', so the dead king could ride along.

Ra also had a temper. In the Book of the Heavenly Cow, humans plot against the ageing sun god, and he sends his Eye, Hathor, to punish them. She turns into the lioness Sekhmet and starts a massacre. To stop her, Ra floods the land with beer dyed red; she drinks it, thinking it blood, gets drunk and becomes gentle Hathor again. Humanity survived because the gods got a goddess drunk.
details: Sun disc with a cobra on a falcon head: Ra or Ra-Horakhty. Scarab for a head: Khepri. Ram head in a boat: the night sun.
Abu Simbel facade (17th): in the niche over the door, falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty stands between signs spelling Ramesses' throne name.
Royal tombs (21st): find the sun disc in its boat and a long snake nearby, Apophis, often pierced by knives.
A king's second cartouche is introduced by a duck and a sun disc: 'Son of Ra', a title every king used from Dynasty 4.
fun_fact: Egyptians said humans were made from Ra's tears: in Egyptian the words for 'people' and 'tears', remetj and remyt, sounded almost the same.
narration: Ra is the sun, and in Egyptian eyes the sun lived a whole life every day. At dawn he was Khepri, a scarab beetle pushing the new sun over the horizon. At noon he was Ra, a falcon headed man with a blazing disc on his head, sailing across the sky in his day boat. At dusk he was Atum, an old man, stepping down into the west. Then came the dangerous part. For the twelve hours of night the sun sailed a dark river under the earth, the Duat, in a night boat, wearing a ram's head. He visited the dead, joined with Osiris, and every night fought Apophis, a giant serpent of chaos who tried to swallow the boat. Seth, of all gods, stood at the prow and speared him. At dawn the sun was born again. That journey is what the painted walls of the Valley of the Kings are about: the dead king rides in Ra's boat and rises with him. From the age of the pyramids, every pharaoh called himself Son of Ra. Ra also had a temper. When humans plotted against him, he sent his Eye, Hathor, who became the lioness Sekhmet and began to slaughter them. To stop her, Ra poured out beer dyed red. She drank it, thinking it was blood, fell asleep drunk, and woke up gentle. In a royal tomb, look for a long snake cut by knives: that is Apophis, losing again.

period: Worshipped from Dynasty 5, c. 2400 BC, to the 6th century AD
summary: Green-skinned, wrapped like a mummy, holding the crook and flail: Osiris judged the dead, and every Egyptian hoped to become him.
look: Osiris wears mummy wrappings from the chest down, has green or black skin, a tall white crown flanked by two ostrich feathers (the atef), and the crook and flail crossed on his chest. In tombs he sits enthroned at the end of a scene, receiving the dead king or the newly judged. The Osiride pillars at Abu Simbel (17th) and Medinet Habu (21st) show the king in his pose.
story:
His Egyptian name was something like Wesir; the Greeks made it Osiris. He appears in the 5th Dynasty, and soon the formula on tomb doors, 'an offering which the king gives to Anubis', became 'to Osiris'. His titles say what he was: Khentiamentiu, 'Foremost of the Westerners', that is, of the dead, and Wennefer, 'the one who remains perfect'.

Green skin means sprouting plants and black means the Nile's fertile mud, because he was also the power in the yearly flood and the growing grain. In the month of Khoiak priests sowed 'Osiris beds', trays of earth in his shape, and watched him sprout; one was found in Tutankhamun's tomb. At Abydos, where his tomb was said to lie, his death and resurrection were staged as a public drama for centuries.

His backbone was the djed pillar, symbol of stability. As judge he presides in the Hall of Two Truths while the heart is weighed. First only kings became Osiris at death; from the Middle Kingdom ordinary people did too, and their texts call them 'the Osiris So-and-so'. Becoming Osiris meant being dead but restored: the best deal Egyptian religion could offer.
details: Crook and flail crossed on a mummiform chest: Osiris, or a king dressed as him, as on Tutankhamun's coffins at the GEM.
Osiride pillars at Abu Simbel (17th) and Medinet Habu (21st): the king wrapped like Osiris, arms crossed, for eternity.
A green face on a coffin lid shows the dead person as Osiris, reborn like spring plants.
Karnak's small Osiris chapels and the Temple of Opet (22nd) celebrated his rebirth inside Amun's own precinct.
fun_fact: Women became Osiris too: a dead woman's coffin could call her 'the Osiris' followed by her name, a male god's title worn without fuss.
narration: Osiris is the god wrapped like a mummy, with green or black skin, a tall white crown with an ostrich feather on each side, and a crook and flail crossed on his chest. He is the murdered king of the myth, put back together by Isis, who became ruler of the dead. His green skin is new plants, his black skin the fertile mud of the Nile. Egyptians saw him in the flood and in the sprouting grain. Priests even planted Osiris beds, trays of earth in his shape sown with grain, and watched him come back to life. One was found in Tutankhamun's tomb. As judge, he sits on his throne at the end of the hall where the heart of the dead is weighed. His backbone was the djed pillar, the sign of stability. At first only dead kings became Osiris. Later everyone could, and texts call the deceased the Osiris so and so. At Abu Simbel and Medinet Habu, look at the pillars: the king stands wrapped and holding crook and flail, dressed as Osiris for eternity.

period: Attested from Dynasty 5, c. 2400 BC; worshipped at Philae until c. AD 537
summary: Horus's mother and the cleverest of the gods, Isis outlived the pharaohs and was worshipped from Philae to Delos, Pompeii and Rome.
look: Isis is a woman with a small throne on her head, the hieroglyph of her name. From the New Kingdom she often wears Hathor's cow horns and sun disc instead, so check the label. She kneels with spread wings at the foot of coffins, nurses the baby Horus on her lap, and is the lady of Philae, whose temple you visit on the 18th or 19th.
story:
Her name, Aset, is written with the throne sign, and some scholars think she began as the throne itself, the 'mother' that made a man a king. She first appears in the 5th Dynasty and grows with the Osiris myth: the wife who searched Egypt for her husband's body, the mourner, the magician who revived him long enough to conceive Horus, and the mother who hid the baby from Seth in the Delta marshes.

She was 'more clever than a million gods'. In one tale she makes a snake from Ra's spittle and earth; it bites him, and she will not cure him until he tells her his secret name. Healing spells cast a sick child as Horus and the healer as Isis. In the New Kingdom she took over much of Hathor's role, horns included.

In the last millennium BC she became Egypt's most popular goddess. Her temple at Philae served Egyptians and Nubians alike and outlasted every other. Greeks made her a protector of sailors and inventor of marriage, and her cult spread around the Mediterranean, with temples on Delos, at Pompeii and in Rome. Images of Isis nursing Horus are often compared with the Virgin and Child, though how far one shaped the other is debated.
details: Throne on the head: Isis. Cow horns with a sun disc: Hathor, unless the label or the scene says Isis.
Winged woman kneeling with arms spread at the foot of a coffin or sarcophagus: Isis protecting the dead.
The tyet, or 'Isis knot', looks like an ankh with drooping arms; amulets of it were often made of red stone.
Philae (18th-19th): Isis's last great temple, with Christian crosses cut into its walls after it was closed.
fun_fact: Late Roman sources say the desert peoples south of Philae were allowed to borrow Isis's statue for their own festivals, one reason her cult there survived so long.
narration: Isis is the goddess with a small throne on her head. That throne is the hieroglyph of her name, and some scholars think she began as the royal throne itself, the mother that turns a man into a king. In the myth, she is the wife who searched all of Egypt for her murdered husband Osiris, put him back together, and conceived their son Horus. Then she hid the baby in the marshes and raised him to take back the throne. She was also the cleverest of the gods. In one story she makes a snake that bites the sun god Ra, and will only cure him if he tells her his secret name. He gives in. Later she borrowed Hathor's cow horns and sun disc, so check the label before you decide which goddess you are looking at. In Greek and Roman times her cult spread across the Mediterranean, to Delos, Pompeii and Rome. Her image nursing Horus may even have shaped pictures of the Madonna and child. At Philae, her last temple, look for crosses carved by Christians on the walls of her house.

period: From late Predynastic times, c. 3200 BC, to the Roman period
summary: The falcon and the mystery beast: their 80-year feud was Egypt's myth of rightful succession, and Seth was never simply the villain.
look: Horus is the falcon, or a man with a falcon's head, often in the double crown; Edfu (20th) is his temple, guarded by granite falcons. Seth has the head of an animal nobody can identify: curved snout, tall square-tipped ears, stiff forked tail. On throne sides you may see the two of them knotting the plants of south and north around the sign for 'unite'.
story:
The falcon's name probably means 'the one far above'. He was the god of Nekhen in the south, and from the beginning the living king was his earthly form. Seth, lord of the red desert, storms, violence and foreigners, balanced him as lord of the black, fertile land.

In the myth Seth murders Osiris, and Horus, son of Isis, claims the throne. The New Kingdom tale 'The Contendings of Horus and Seth' turns their trial into farce: the case drags on for 80 years because the judge, Ra, favours Seth; they race boats and fight as hippos; Seth tears out Horus's eye and Horus damages Seth's testicles; Isis tricks Seth into condemning himself. Horus wins, as the rightful son must.

Seth was more than a villain. Every night he stood in the prow of Ra's boat and speared the serpent Apophis. The Hyksos made him their chief god, and the Ramesside kings came from his cult centre in the Delta: Seti means 'man of Seth'. Only after Libyan, Nubian, Assyrian and Persian conquests was he demonised as the god of hated foreigners, and his images hacked away. The Greeks equated him with Typhon, the monster that fought Zeus.
details: Seth animal: down-curved snout, square-topped ears, forked tail. Aardvark, donkey and wild dog have been proposed; none fits.
Edfu (20th): granite falcons of Horus flank the pylon entrance; the best one, in the double crown, stands at the hypostyle door.
Throne sides: two gods knotting papyrus and lily around a windpipe sign. Sometimes Nile gods, sometimes Horus and Seth.
Edfu's west wall: Horus harpoons Seth, shrunk to a small hippo so he cannot harm the temple.
fun_fact: Ramesses II set up a stela celebrating 400 years of Seth's cult in the Delta: the god of chaos got an anniversary party.
narration: Horus is the falcon, and Seth is the strange animal with a curved snout, tall square ears and a stiff forked tail that nobody has ever matched to a real beast. Aardvark, donkey and wild dog have all been suggested. Horus was the sky and the king: every living pharaoh was Horus on earth. Seth was the red desert, storms and foreigners. In the myth, Seth murders his brother Osiris, and Horus, the son, claims the throne. A New Kingdom story turns their court case into a comedy: it drags on for 80 years, they race boats, fight as hippos, Seth tears out Horus's eye, and Isis tricks Seth into condemning himself. Horus wins, because the rightful son must. But Seth was not simply evil. Every night he stood at the front of the sun's boat and speared the chaos serpent. The Ramesside kings came from his cult centre, and Seti means man of Seth. Only after foreign invasions was he turned into a devil. At Edfu on the 20th, find the granite falcon at the gate: that is Horus himself.

period: Anubis from Dynasty 1, c. 3000 BC; Thoth from the Old Kingdom; both to the Roman period
summary: One guards the cemetery and wraps the dead; the other invented writing and keeps the gods' minutes. Together they run the judgement of the soul.
look: Anubis is the black jackal lying on a shrine, or a man with a jackal's head bending over a mummy or adjusting the scales. Thoth has the long curved beak of an ibis, often with a moon disc on a crescent, and holds a scribe's palette; he can also appear as a baboon. Both stand at the weighing of the heart in tomb paintings and Book of the Dead papyri.
story:
The jackal god, Egyptian Inpu, appears from the 1st Dynasty. Jackals dug up shallow graves at the desert edge, so Egyptians set a jackal to guard the dead: fight like with like. His black is not the animal's colour but that of the resin-soaked mummy and of fertile Nile mud, meaning rebirth. His titles describe the job: 'He who is upon his mountain', watching the necropolis; 'He who is in the place of embalming'. He embalmed Osiris, priests in jackal masks played him at funerals, and at the judgement he checks the scales. The Greeks merged him with Hermes, guide of souls, as Hermanubis.

Thoth, Djehuty, was the moon, reckoner of time, inventor of writing and scribe of the gods. His animals were the ibis and the baboon, whose chatter at sunrise looked like greeting the sun. He mediated between Horus and Seth, restored Horus's torn eye, gave Isis the words to revive Osiris, and records the verdict on the dead. His city was Hermopolis, whose huge temple porch was still standing in 1826, before it was demolished to fill a sugar factory's foundations. Greeks called him Hermes Trismegistus, 'thrice great', and later alchemists and mystics claimed his secret books.
details: Black jackal lying on a chest or shrine: Anubis guarding the tomb, as on Tutankhamun's Anubis shrine at the GEM.
Ibis head with a moon disc on a crescent, pen and palette in hand: Thoth writing down the verdict.
Abu Simbel facade (17th): along the very top runs a row of baboons raising their hands to the rising sun.
Luxor Temple (22nd): look at the base of the obelisk by the pylon for baboons greeting the sun.
fun_fact: In Plato's Gorgias, Socrates swears 'by the dog, the god of the Egyptians': Anubis made it into Greek philosophy.
narration: Two gods run the judgement of the dead. Anubis is the black jackal, or a man with a jackal's head. Jackals dug up shallow graves at the desert edge, so Egyptians set a jackal to guard the dead: fight like with like. But his black is not the colour of jackals. It is the colour of a mummy soaked in resin, and of the fertile Nile mud, which means rebirth. He embalmed Osiris, the first mummy, and at funerals a priest wearing a jackal mask played his part. At the weighing of the heart, Anubis checks the scales. Thoth is the ibis, or sometimes a baboon. He is the moon, the inventor of writing and the scribe of the gods, and he writes down the verdict. He also healed the torn eye of Horus. The Greeks matched Thoth with Hermes and called him Hermes Trismegistus, thrice great. And Socrates, in Plato, swears by the dog, the god of the Egyptians. At Abu Simbel on the 17th, look up along the top of the facade: a row of baboons raises its hands to greet the rising sun.

period: Prominent from Dynasty 4, c. 2600 BC, to the Roman period
summary: Goddess of love, music, beer and the sky, Hathor could also become a lioness that nearly wiped out humanity. No goddess had more temples.
look: Hathor is a woman with cow horns curving around a sun disc, or a cow, or a calm woman's face with cow's ears on top of a column. Those Hathor capitals are in the Small Temple at Abu Simbel (17th), Hatshepsut's Hathor chapel (21st) and at Philae (18th). She shakes a sistrum rattle or holds a heavy menat necklace, and in the Theban hills she is a cow stepping out of the western mountain to receive the dead.
story:
Her name, Hut-Hor, means 'House of Horus': she was the sky in which the falcon lived, or the womb from which the sun was born each day. Cow goddesses go back to prehistory, but Hathor rose with the pyramid kings of Dynasty 4 to become Ra's wife and the divine mother of the king. Her great temple was at Dendera, north of Luxor, and more temples were dedicated to her than to any other goddess.

She was the 'Golden One' of love, sex, beauty, music, dance, perfume and drunkenness. A text at Edfu says the gods play the sistrum for her 'to dispel her bad temper'. That temper is the other half of her story. As the Eye of Ra she was sent to punish rebellious humans, became the lioness Sekhmet and began a massacre, until Ra flooded the land with red-dyed beer. The Festival of Drunkenness re-enacted her calming, and at the Temple of Mut in Karnak excavators found a 'porch of drunkenness' built by Hatshepsut.

In the Theban necropolis she was 'Mistress of the West', the cow emerging from the mountain, and the sycamore that gave the dead food and water. She nursed kings: at Deir el-Bahari a relief shows Hatshepsut suckled by the Hathor cow. The 'Seven Hathors' appeared at births to announce a child's fate. Ramesses II dedicated the Small Temple at Abu Simbel to her and to Nefertari, who wears her horns and disc. The Greeks equated her with Aphrodite.
details: Abu Simbel Small Temple (17th): pillars topped with Hathor's face and cow ears, and Nefertari wearing her horned crown.
Hatshepsut's temple (21st): in the Hathor chapel, Hathor-faced capitals and the queen suckled by the divine cow.
Philae (18th): the small Hathor temple shows musicians, and Bes dancing and playing for her.
Sistrum: a rattle with Hathor's face on the handle. Menat: a heavy bead necklace with a counterweight, shaken in her rites.
fun_fact: Texts speak of 'Seven Hathors' who turned up at a birth to pronounce the baby's fate, rather like the fairies at Sleeping Beauty's christening.
narration: Hathor is the goddess with cow horns curving around a sun disc, or simply a cow, or a woman's face with cow ears on top of a column. Her name means House of Horus: she was the sky that held the falcon, and the mother of the sun. She was the Golden One, goddess of love, beauty, music, dance, perfume and drunkenness, and more temples were built for her than for any other goddess. Musicians shook rattles called sistra to keep her happy, and one text admits why: to drive away her bad temper. Because Hathor had a dark side. When humans plotted against the sun god Ra, he sent her as his Eye to punish them. She turned into Sekhmet, a lioness, and began to slaughter everyone. To save humanity, Ra flooded the fields with beer dyed red. She drank it, thinking it was blood, got gloriously drunk, and turned back into sweet Hathor. Egyptians celebrated with a Festival of Drunkenness, and Hatshepsut built a porch of drunkenness at Karnak for it. In Thebes she was also Mistress of the West, a cow stepping out of the mountain to welcome the dead. She nursed kings, and the Greeks called her Aphrodite. At Abu Simbel's Small Temple on the 17th, look for the pillars topped with her calm face and cow ears.

period: Ptah from the Early Dynastic Period; Sekhmet from Dynasty 5; both to the Roman period
summary: The craftsman god who created the world by speaking it, and his wife, a lioness whose breath was the desert wind. Egypt itself is named after his temple.
look: Ptah stands wrapped like a mummy with his hands free, a tight skullcap, a straight beard and a staff combining the was, ankh and djed signs. Sekhmet is a woman with a lioness's head and a sun disc. You meet Ptah in the dark of Abu Simbel's sanctuary (17th) and in his small temple at Karnak, where a black Sekhmet stands alone in a shrine (22nd).
story:
His home was Memphis, the old capital. A text carved on the Shabaka Stone around 700 BC says he created the gods 'through this heart and this tongue', conceiving things and naming them, an idea often compared with 'In the beginning was the Word'. He was patron of craftsmen, architects and sculptors; the sage Imhotep was later called his son, and the tomb-builders of Thebes prayed to 'Ptah who listens to prayers'. His Memphis temple, Hut-ka-Ptah, 'enclosure of the ka of Ptah', became Greek Aigyptos and our 'Egypt'. Greeks matched him with Hephaestus.

Sekhmet, 'the Powerful', was his wife, a daughter of Ra and his Eye at its most violent. She breathed fire, her breath was the hot desert wind, and plagues were her messengers. The same power could heal, and she was invoked against disease. Amenhotep III had around 700 statues of her carved, perhaps more; many now stand in the Precinct of Mut at Karnak and in museums worldwide. Their son was Nefertem, the young god of the lotus, often with a lotus flower on his head.
details: Abu Simbel sanctuary (17th): four seated gods. Ptah, at the left end, is the one the sunbeam never reaches.
Karnak, Temple of Ptah (22nd): Sekhmet stands in a dark shrine lit only by a hole in the roof.
Rows of black granite Sekhmets, seated or standing, come from Amenhotep III; you will meet them in museums and at Mut's precinct.
Ptah's staff stacks three signs: was for power, ankh for life, djed for stability.
Tutankhamun's head rising from a lotus at the GEM shows him as Nefertem, the child god born from the flower.
fun_fact: The word 'Egypt' is Ptah's: his Memphis temple, Hut-ka-Ptah, became the Greek Aigyptos, so every Greek saying 'Aigyptos' is naming a god's house.
narration: Ptah is the god wrapped like a mummy, with a tight skullcap and a straight beard, holding a staff that stacks three signs: power, life and stability. He was the god of Memphis, the old capital, and the patron of craftsmen and sculptors. One text says he created the world by thinking of it in his heart and speaking it with his tongue, a bit like In the beginning was the Word. His temple at Memphis was called Hut ka Ptah, the house of Ptah's spirit. The Greeks heard it as Aigyptos, and that is where the word Egypt comes from. They matched him with their own smith god, Hephaestus. His wife Sekhmet, the Powerful, is a woman with a lioness's head. Her breath was the hot desert wind and plague was her messenger, yet she was also called on to heal the sick. Amenhotep the Third had around 700 statues of her carved to keep her calm. At Abu Simbel's sanctuary on the 17th, look at the god on the far left: that is Ptah, the one the sunbeam never reaches.

summary: A potter, a crocodile, a fertility god with lettuce, a war falcon and two southern goddesses: the local gods of the places on this trip.
look: Khnum has a ram's head with long wavy horizontal horns and often sits at a potter's wheel; Sobek has a crocodile's head. Min stands stiffly with an erect phallus, one arm raised with a flail and two tall plumes on his head; Montu is a falcon with two plumes and a sun disc. Satet wears the white crown with antelope horns, Anuket a tall crown of feathers.
story: Every town had its own god. At Aswan's First Cataract, Khnum the ram controlled the flood and shaped people on a potter's wheel, with the goddesses Satet and Anuket; you will see his temple ruins on Elephantine (18th-19th) and his Roman-period hall at Esna (20th). Sobek the crocodile shares Kom Ombo with Horus. Min of Koptos ruled fertility and harvest; lettuce, whose milky sap suggested semen, was his plant, eaten for potency. Montu was Thebes' war god before Amun. Above the Valley of the Kings, the cobra Meretseger, 'she who loves silence', guarded the peak.
details: Min on Karnak and Luxor walls: stiff figure, erect phallus, raised flail, tall plumes, often with lettuces behind him.
Khnum at his potter's wheel shaping a royal child: in Hatshepsut's birth scenes (21st) and at Luxor Temple (22nd).
Kom Ombo (20th): one half of the twin temple is Sobek's; mummified crocodiles wait in the museum next door.
Esna (20th): Khnum's hymns credit him with shaping gods, people, animals and plants.
fun_fact: Khufu's full name was Khnum-Khufwy, 'Khnum protects me': the builder of the Great Pyramid was named after the potter god.
narration: Every town had its own god, and this trip passes through their homes. At Aswan, Khnum, the ram with long wavy horns, controlled the Nile flood and shaped every child on his potter's wheel, helped by the goddesses Satet and Anuket. At Kom Ombo, Sobek the crocodile shares a double temple with Horus. Min, the stiff god with the raised flail and the very obvious erection, was lord of fertility. His sacred plant was lettuce, eaten for potency. Montu, a falcon, was the war god of Thebes before Amun. At Esna on the 20th, look for Khnum's ram head among the Roman columns.
